reading.title: Inside a Neighborhood Farmers Market
reading.purpose: Explore how everyday market booths show big economic forces at work.
paras: Every Saturday morning, an empty parking lot turns into a lively center of commerce, where dozens of growers and bakers buy, sell, and trade goods with local families. Each shopper who walks between the tents with a canvas tote is a consumer deciding how to spend limited cash. Behind the tables stand small growers, cheesemakers, and at least one young entrepreneur who risked personal savings to launch a brand-new salsa stand.

Running a booth takes more than fresh fruit. Owners must invest money upfront in seeds, jars, and sturdy tables before earning a single dollar back. They also depend on human labor, the steady physical work of planting, picking, washing, and packing crates before dawn. When a farm hires high school helpers to weigh apples and make change, it pays each worker an hourly wage that must fit inside the day's budget.

Prices at the market shift for clear reasons. After a late spring frost ruins half the peach crop, scarcity sets in because there is not enough fruit to meet demand, and each basket costs more. Over several years, inflation can also lift prices across the whole market, meaning a ten-dollar bill buys fewer loaves and berries than it once did.

Even national policies reach the parking lot. A baker who buys imported vanilla or cinnamon may pay more if a new tariff adds a tax on goods brought from another country. On the other hand, a state subsidy, money a government gives to support local growers, can help a small orchard buy water-saving pipes and keep cider prices steady. Watching one Saturday market reveals how choices made on farms, in kitchens, and in capitals all connect.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "subsidy" most nearly means
choices: a tax placed on spices shipped from another country
a shortage of fruit caused by a late spring frost
money a government gives to support a business or grower
an hourly payment earned by a helper at a market booth
qs.why: Paragraph 4 defines subsidy directly as "money a government gives to support local growers."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how weather can raise the price of a market item?
choices: Prices at the market shift for clear reasons.
After a late spring frost ruins half the peach crop, scarcity sets in because there is not enough fruit to meet demand, and each basket costs more.
Over several years, inflation can also lift prices across the whole market, meaning a ten-dollar bill buys fewer loaves and berries than it once did.
Watching one Saturday market reveals how choices made on farms, in kitchens, and in capitals all connect.
qs.why: This sentence connects a late spring frost directly to a peach shortage and higher basket prices.

ev.text: After a late spring frost ruins half the peach crop, scarcity sets in because there is not enough fruit to meet demand, and each basket costs more.

qs.q: Why might a small farm owner think carefully before hiring extra Saturday helpers?
choices: Extra helpers usually refuse to weigh apples or pack crates before dawn.
The owner must pay each worker an hourly wage from the booth's budget.
Local shoppers prefer to buy fruit only from booths with a single worker.
State laws prevent high school students from working at outdoor markets.
qs.why: Paragraph 2 notes that paying an hourly wage must fit inside the day's budget, alongside upfront investments.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Local farmers markets are cheaper than grocery stores because they never face inflation or taxes.
Starting a new salsa stand is the easiest way for a young person to avoid financial risk.
A neighborhood farmers market shows how work, shortages, and government rules shape prices.
Imported vanilla and cinnamon should be replaced with local fruit at every Saturday market.
qs.why: The reading uses a local farmers market to illustrate commerce, labor, scarcity, inflation, tariffs, and subsidies.
